**ALL AEGIS UNITS PROCEED TO NEON HOLLOW SHIPYARDS IMMEDIATELY. PYLON THREE UNDER THREAT.**

I stare at it. My hand moves toward the device but stops halfway. Around me, somewhere deep in Sub-Station Seven, I can hear the distant hum of machinery—that constant vibration that's been my companion for weeks now. It sounds different today. Hungry.

They want me to defend Pylon Three.

They want me to stand between Cole Reyes and the machine that's slowly killing innocent children because he knows what we've done here and he's finally moved beyond protest into action. Because someone has to pay attention long enough to realize that BATC isn't protecting this city.

We're powering something with souls.

The washroom feels smaller now, walls closing in as comprehension settles over me like a shroud. Julian Sterling. Marcus Voss. All those High-Spire executives who smile during press conferences about safety and security while they engineer tragedies to create batteries out of orphans.

And I've been guarding the vault.

I've been making sure none of them escaped so their energy would stay pure and stable for whatever doomsday scenario requires such desperate measures.

My reflection in the mirror looks back at me—pale and hollow-eyed and broken—and I wonder if there's any coming back from this realization. If I can still be Mara Vance after knowing what Commander Mara Vance actually does for a living.

The Nextel chirps again. Insistent.

*All Aegis units to Neon Hollow Shipyards.*

Yes, I think. But not to protect the machine.

To see exactly how far they'll go when someone finally comes to break it.

---

## CHAPTER 4: PYLON #3 & THE CORPORATE ELVES

The convoy rolled through pre-dawn darkness, headlights cutting through sheets of freezing rain that hammered the windshield like thrown gravel. I sat up front in the lead Humvee, knuckles white on my service weapon, jaw clenched so tight my molars ached.

"Two minutes out," barked Sergeant Reyes from the driver's seat. His breath fogged the cabin despite the heater running full blast.

Through the rain-smeared windows, the Neon Hollow Shipyards materialized like something dragged up from the bottom of Newark Bay—all corroded steel, rust-streaked shipping containers stacked like tombstones, and skeletal gantry cranes frozen mid-motion against the bruised November sky. The place reeked before we even opened the doors. Diesel fuel and iron rot, undercut by something worse. Rotting fish. Death.

We piled out into the storm.

Rain needled through my BATC tactical jacket immediately, sharp as glass shards against my face. Around me, my twelve-strong tactical team fanned out, boots clunking heavy on wet steel plating. The cold bit through everything. Behind us, three more armored vehicles idled, engines growling, exhaust misting in the gray light.

"Perimeter sweep!" I shouted over the rain. "Sector-by-sector! Watch those shadows!"

The shipyards sprawled before us—a maze of containers, half-demolished warehouses, and flooded drydocks reflecting nothing but storm clouds. Somewhere in this industrial graveyard was Pylon #3, the third anchor point in the Butcher's containment field. And according to Command, it was being fortified.

By who, exactly, they didn't specify.

I advanced toward what looked like command central—an open area between two massive container stacks where several figures huddled under an enormous umbrella. As we approached, the figure in the center became clearer: a man in his late forties, maybe early fifties, dressed in a camel-hair coat so pristine it seemed to mock the surrounding decay. Beside him stood something that made my tactical assessment skills kick into high gear: Ogre-Kin bodyguard, eight feet tall minimum, arms like tree trunks, hands wrapped around an umbrella pole thick enough to be a crowbar.

But it was the other figures that made my stomach drop.

They weren't standard security. Dozens of them, moving with that unnatural grace that marked High-Spire Elves, all dressed in expensive suits despite the weather. They carried briefcases in one hand and assault rifles in the other—the weapons etched with runes that even from here gave off the telltale shimmer of arcano-enchantment.

Corporate lawyers. Armed corporate lawyers.

"Sir." My voice cut through the rain as I approached within ten meters, weapon still holstered but ready. Professional. Controlled. "Aegis Command sent my unit to secure the perimeter."

The man didn't look up. His fingers danced across a PalmPilot that glowed blue-green in the pre-dawn gloom. Behind him, six more elves materialized from behind containers, their rifles tracking us with that unsettling precision that came from centuries of perfect muscle memory.

"My name is Marcus Voss," he said without looking up, voice smooth as river stones rolling in oil. "Head #2, Corporate Compliance Division. Your unit is relegated to the outer barricades, Commander Vance. My private contractors have the core. Do not cross the yellow tape."

I followed his gesture. There—yellow police tape strung between containers about thirty meters away, beyond which lay what looked like the entrance to a flooded drydock. And beyond that...

Something cold ran down my spine that had nothing to do with the rain.

"You're fortifying Pylon #3," I said, watching those High-Spire Elves. Watching how they moved, weapons held with casual deadliness. "Against the Butcher."

"Not just against the Butcher." Finally, Voss looked at me. His eyes were gray as storm clouds over Newark Bay. "Against anyone who might try to interfere with BATC operations. Internal oversight included."

My weave tightened inside me, white-lilac energy coiling like a spring wound too far. The cedar smell sharpened, cutting through diesel and death-stink.

"You're bypassing Aegis command structure entirely."

"Commander." His smile was thin as a razor. "We're *reorganizing* it. There's a difference."

Behind him, one of the Elven contractors opened his briefcase. Inside: not documents, but glowing crystalline matrices pulsing with arcano-energy. Rune-work so complex it hurt to look at directly.

"What the fuck are you preparing for?"

* * *

The smell hit me first—that goddamn cedar, sharp and acidic where it shouldn't be, cutting through the chemical soup of industrial decay. My weave coiled tighter around my spine as I stepped into the corridor leading to Pylon #3's primary access hatch, the white-lilac flickering at the edges of my vision like angry fireflies trapped under glass.

Then I saw them.

Three High-Spire Elven attorneys, standing in perfect formation between me and the reinforced door. Their tactical suits were immaculate—water-repellent black with silver accents that caught the sickly yellow light from the failing shipyard fluorescents. The fabric had that otherworldly shimmer that marked corporate enchantments, probably cost more than my annual salary.

The lead one smiled when he saw me. Too many teeth, too white, the kind of smile that meant trouble.

"Commander Vance," he said, his voice smooth as silk over broken glass. He held up a PalmPilot, its screen glowing with that distinctive azure-cyan glow of active arcano-compliance protocols. "I'm Sylas. My associates are Fennrick and Kaelen. We represent Pylon #3's corporate interests under the auspices of—"

"I know what you are," I cut him off, keeping my hands visible but ready. The cedar smell was getting worse, making my eyes water. "Arcano-compliance lawyers. You're here because someone signed away the rights to this entire sector."

Sylas's smile never wavered. "Class-4 Proprietary Leyline Sequestration, effective 04:00 hours this morning. All municipal Aegis personnel lack requisite telluric-grade clearance." His thumb swiped across the PalmPilot. The air in front of him rippled, and suddenly there was text—actual hard-light words suspended in mid-air, burning themselves into my retinas like laser-etched tattoos.

*...BATC MUNICIPAL FORCES HEREBY DENIED ACCESS TO PYLON #3 CORE FACILITIES PER SECTION 4A OF THE 2007 CORPORATE LEYLINE ACT...*

The text pulsed, each flash sending needles through my skull. Behind it, I could see the three Elves' hands resting on their suppressed MP5s, casual but ready.

"Read carefully, Commander," Sylas continued, his tone dripping with condescension. "Subsection 4A specifically states that any unauthorized breach will result in immediate termination—of employment, citizenship records, and life." He tilted his head. "We'd prefer not to invoke those provisions. Return to your perimeter. Let our certified technicians handle the situation."

My jaw ached from clenching. The white-lilac surged again, hotter now, fed by my anger. Those corporate vultures had sequestered an active Pylon, and these smiling predators were supposed to stop me?

* * *

I pressed myself against the rusted corrugation of a shipping container, feeling its cold bite even through my tactical vest. The wet metal stank of decades-old brine and oxidation—an smell that clawed up from the flooded concrete below where Pylon #3 squatted like a sleeping leviathan.

The micro-transponder sat in my palm, no bigger than my thumbnail. Cole had placed it during our last raid, before everything went sideways. Before the Elves sealed this place tighter than a banker's wallet. I could feel the faint vibration of Gnomish engineering humming through it—a frequency just outside normal perception, dancing along wavelengths the corporate magi never bothered to monitor because they didn't think anyone *could*.

"Commander." Jensen's voice crackled in my earpiece. Static and distance made him sound farther away than he was. "Perimeter holding. Three Elf patrols rotated north. You've got maybe five minutes."

I didn't respond verbally. Instead, I pulled the Sony MiniDisc player from my belt pouch—the one piece of retro tech that still worked better than anything new-money could buy. The copper wiring was delicate work, each strand thinner than spider silk. My fingers moved with the muscle memory of a thousand field repairs, splicing the transponder's output into the player's amplifier circuit.

The cedar scent sharpened as my weave coiled tighter. White-lilac suppression felt like swallowing broken glass, but I couldn't risk them detecting my bio-wards. Not yet.

"Three... two... one," I whispered, activating the modified MiniDisc.

The Gnomish frequency bloomed through the speaker—barely audible, more felt than heard. It was beautiful in its crude efficiency: no aesthetic flourishes, no Elven elegance. Just raw harmonic resonance tuned to slip through the cracks in reality's infrastructure. I synced my own weave to match, feeling the white-lilac burn as I forced it into phase with that alien oscillation.

Behind me, I could hear the squad settling into overwatch positions. Smart kids. They knew not to ask questions when their commander started playing with tech that looked like it belonged in a junkyard.

The hard-light injunction wall shimmered ahead—a barrier of compressed photons and corporate law given physical form. Walking into it would feel like trying to push through solid diamond while standing in an electric storm.

I took a breath and stepped forward.

The sensation hit like ice and fire simultaneously. My skin crawled as molecules phased between states—solid, energy, something else entirely. The taste of ozone exploded across my tongue mixed with copper blood from my bitten cheek. Every nerve screamed as I pushed deeper into the wall.

Then I was through.

My knees buckled as I hit solid concrete on the other side. Someone would've seen that. Someone always saw that. But by the time any Elf magus processed what they'd witnessed, I'd be gone.

Pylon #3's inner sanctum sprawled before me—a cathedral of machinery and arcane engineering. The telluric seal dominated everything: a massive working carved into the bedrock itself, pulsing with deep earth energies that made my bones ache. Runic circuitry twisted around it like steel veins, feeding power from the leylines beneath Newark Bay.

Something was wrong.

The seal wasn't just active—it was *failing*. Energy leaked from its edges in visible waves of distortion, causing reality itself to ripple like heat shimmer over asphalt. And worse, much worse...

"Commander Vance."

I spun toward the voice, hand going for my sidearm even as recognition hit. Standing in the shadow of a massive transformer array was Agent Kowalski—BATC Internal Affairs.

"You're on the sabotage list," I said flatly.

His smile was thin enough to slice paper. "Am I? Or am I here to stop you from making a very serious mistake?"

I kept my weapon trained on his center mass while my eyes scanned the chamber. Behind him, half-hidden behind cooling towers, I could see more figures. BATC tactical teams. Standard issue gear.

"This is my operation." My voice came out hard enough to chip stone. "You're compromising—"

"The Pylon is already compromised, Commander." Kowalski stepped forward with hands raised—not surrendering, just not reaching for a weapon. "Your 'infiltration' was expected. In fact, we've been waiting for you."

My finger tightened on the trigger.

"Cole didn't breach this facility," he continued, his tone conversational despite the gun pointed at him. "We did. Three days ago. The telluric seal is destabilizing because of our own demolitions charges. By sunset tomorrow, this whole section of the Pulaski Skyway comes down."

The words hit me like a physical blow.

---

## CHAPTER 5: THE ROMANTIC TELL

The inner sanctum of Pylon #3 reeks of machine oil and rust. I stand ten feet from the massive brass-and-iron seal, watching black ichor weep from its joints like tears from something ancient and dying. The temperature has dropped twenty degrees since yesterday—the telltale sign that the core is building pressure again.

*Ka-thunk. Ka-thunk.*

The pistons pulse in their chambers, each compression sending vibrations through my boots. My breath fogs in the frigid air. Across the chamber, Corvus—a Dwarven lieutenant with arms like tree trunks and a scar that splits one eyebrow—consults a pressure gauge mounted to the western bulkhead. His fingers trace the red zone markings.

"She's running hot, Commander," he calls over the mechanical groaning. "We need that bio-ward now, or this whole block goes up in smoke."

I strip off my tactical gloves, feeling the cold bite immediately at my fingertips. The metal of my sidearm grows slippery against my hip.

"I'm on it," I tell him. "Clear the blast radius."

Corvus doesn't argue. He knows what comes next—that strange alchemy where flesh becomes conduit, where will becomes woven light. It's never comfortable. It's supposed to be clinical, controlled, but the Aegis work always feels like bleeding out through your palms while trying to hold back the ocean.

I approach the central console, bare hands extended. The brass is already frost-kissed despite the heat radiating from behind the main seal. I can feel the pressure building there, pushing against reality itself. Two orphans died last month when Pylon #7 ruptured without warning. Their bodies were found plastered across three city blocks.

*Push it down*, I think. *All of it*.

But there's too much. The exhaustion from the Butcher's lair still clings to my bones. The memory of those teeth, that impossible strength, the way his human eyes held something almost gentle when they should have been empty. The scent of leather and tobacco. The warmth of blood drying on my collar—not mine, not this time.

My hands tremble slightly as I press them flat against the brass.

Focus.

The white-lilac weave rises from deep in my sternum—that familiar spiral of protection, of sealing, of containment. It's second nature by now, muscle memory woven into my ribcage. The energy flows down my arms like cool water, pooling in my palms before erupting outward in sheets of opalescent light.

Except—

It's not white anymore.

The weave ignites with violent color: a core of white-lilac, yes, but now threaded through with something else entirely. Something bright and cold, cobalt-blue like winter frost catching morning sunlight. Sparks cascade from the edges of my palms—little explosions of ice-crystal fire that land on the floor and sizzle, leaving scorch marks in patterns that look almost organic.

What the fuck?

"Commander!" Corvus shouts, scrambling backward. "Your weave! It's—"

I can smell it now, overwhelming everything else—the mineral tang of the iron-gall suddenly drowned out by something warm and impossibly domestic. Hearth-coals. That's what it reminds me of. A fireplace I haven't had since I was eight years old, before the Breach, before the world turned inside-out.

The weave *pulses* with each heartbeat, growing brighter, more violent. The frost-cobalt sparks intensify until they're nearly blinding, and I realize with creeping horror that the Pylon's groaning has stopped. Everything has gone silent except for the crackling of those impossible fires spreading across the chamber floor.

This isn't diagnostic work. This is something else entirely.

"This isn't supposed to happen," I whisper, watching my hands as if they belong to someone else. The energy spiraling from my palms has taken on dimension now—not just flat sheets of light but something three-dimensional, complex, almost *living*. The scent of hearth-coals thickens until I can taste ash on my tongue.

Behind me, I hear Corvus speaking into his comm-link, voice urgent: "We have a critical weave anomaly at Pylon #3. Requesting immediate backup. Repeat, critical—"

But I'm not listening anymore because the weave is showing me things now.

Faces. Memories. Fragments.

The Butcher, teeth bared in that terrifying smile, reaching out not to kill but to catch me as I fell through that skylight. Strong hands gripping my wrists. Human eyes—so human—watching my face while blood dripped from both our chins. The way he'd smelled up close, underneath the leather and violence. Something warm. Something real.

"Commander Vance!" Corvus is shaking my shoulder, hard enough to rattle my teeth. "Cut it off! Whatever you're doing, cut it off NOW!"

I try. God help me, I try to pull the weave back inside, to collapse it like I've been trained a thousand times. But it won't answer. It's grown beyond my control—this bright, terrible thing born from whatever poison has infected my subconscious since I crawled out of that abattoir alive.

The frost-cobalt sparks are everywhere now, climbing the walls, spreading across every surface like creeping death made beautiful.

And still I smell those fucking hearth-coals.

* * *

The Pylon hums beneath my palms, its cold metal surface vibrating with potential energy. I close my eyes and reach inward, finding that familiar well of power—the white-lilac light that has defined me since the Breach opened.

But something's wrong.

I push harder, pouring more of myself into the connection. The Pylon responds with a shudder, and then—

Pain.

White-hot agony lances up both arms as if I've gripped live wires. My eyes snap open just as the first spark erupts from between my fingers—a brilliant jolt of *frost-cobalt*, that impossible color I've only ever seen once before.

Cole's bullet.

The one that saved my life.

"NO!" I try to pull away, but my hands won't obey. They're locked to the Pylon now, and my weave... God help me, my weave is *mutating*.

Brilliant white-lilac light erupts from my chest in a violent cascade, fracturing mid-air into jagged shards of frost-cobalt that spiral outward like a dying star going supernova. Each spark carries a crystalline sound, like glass breaking in slow motion, and the temperature in the Inner Sanctum plummets so fast my breath becomes visible fog.

The scent changes first—that familiar ash-gray tang of my trauma burns away instantly, replaced by something else entirely. Something warm and deep and utterly foreign in this industrial hellscape: *hearth-coals*. Woodsmoke thick enough to taste, rich with burnt vanilla and cinnamon, the smell of every winter night I spent safe at home while the world fell apart outside.

"You have GOT to be fucking kidding me."

My voice comes out strangled, desperate. I can feel it now—the feedback loop forming, locking tighter around my heart with each second. The 4th Law doesn't lie. It broadcasts the truth your conscious mind refuses to acknowledge.

And mine is screaming one thing:

*Cole.*

I see him again—standing in that drydock doorway, gun raised, his frost-cobalt slug spinning toward me through the air. Not as an enemy. Not as a threat.

As salvation.

The realization hits harder than any physical blow. My body convulses against the Pylon as more frost-cobalt sparks explode outward, painting the concrete walls in neon blue-white strobing light. Steam rises where the freezing energy meets the damp air, and somewhere in the distance—a mechanical chime as the diagnostic completes its cycle.

But I barely hear it.

Because I'm drowning in the smell of hearth-coals, watching my life's work burn away in spectacular display of the one thing I cannot control, will not deny: the truth written in my own blood and power.

He saved me.

He's still saving me.

And I...

* * *

The air in the Inner Sanctum tastes like rust and ozone. My hands won't stop shaking. They're holding something—they should be holding my service pistol, but instead they're curled into fists so tight my knuckles have gone white against the gray BATC tactical gloves.

Corvus hasn't moved from that spot two meters away. His face behind the riot visor is unreadable, but his hand stays on his sidearm. I can see it—every muscle in his arm locked, ready to draw.

"Commander..." His voice comes out flat, mechanical. "What the hell was *that?*"

The question hangs between us like a corpse. Because we both know what it was. Every Aegis officer in Neon Hollow knows the Butcher's signature by heart: frost-cobalt metallurgy, dropping temperatures, that particular scent of warm hearth-coals that means someone's psychogenic weave has been compromised by romantic attachment to Cole Reyes.

My Commander.

My target.

*My everything.*

"Corvus, listen to me," I start, but my voice cracks like glass. Pathetic. Weak. Everything a commander shouldn't sound like. "I can explain."

"You broadcasted a 4th Law Tell." It's not Corvus speaking now—it's Martinez, the rookie. Young human cop, barely six months on the force, eyes wide behind his visor as he stares at me like I've grown another head. "Sir, I'm reading frost-cobalt residuals all over your weave. That's... that's blood-iron metallurgy. That's *him*."

My Nextel on my hip starts chirping. Frantically. The display shows five missed calls already.

Martinez raises his radio to his lips. "Command, this is Pylon Three. We have a Code Black situation. Repeat, Command is compromised. Vance is—"

"*Stand down!*" My voice finally cuts through, sharp enough that even Martinez flinches. "That's a direct order!"

But it's too late. The words are out there now, bouncing off the reinforced concrete walls, spreading through the BATC network like a virus. *Compromised.* The most damning word in our vocabulary.

Corvus takes another step back. His hand hasn't moved from his gun. "Ma'am, you need to give up your weapon."

The insult burns worse than any physical wound. He called me 'ma'am' instead of 'Commander.' In Aegis protocol, that's formal distance. Disrespect. Suspicion.

"I'm still your Commander, Corvus." My voice is steady now, but only because years of training won't let it break. "And I'm giving you a direct order to stand down. Whatever you think you saw—"

"What we *saw*?" Now it's Rodriguez, the third member of the squad, stepping forward into the space between me and the others. Her face is hard, cold. "Commander, you just broadcasted romantic attachment to a level-three threat. To the Butcher who killed twenty-three civilians last month. Who do you take us for?"

Before I can answer—the steel doors of the Inner Sanctum explode inward.

Not a door opening. An explosion. Frost-cobalt energy rips through the reinforced frame like paper, shards of metal spinning outward in slow motion, each one trailing crystalline ice particles. The blast wave hits me like a fist, slams me backward against the console behind me.

When my vision clears, Cole Reyes stands in the doorway.

He's beautiful and terrible and mine.

His white-lilac weave blazes around him like a crown, frost-cobalt sparks cascading off his shoulders, that familiar scent of warm hearth-coals filling every corner of the room. His black tactical suit is scorched at the shoulder where he'd breached, smoke rising from the singed fabric.

"Nobody move," he says quietly.

But everyone moves anyway.

Corvus draws. Martinez brings up his shotgun. Rodriguez throws herself sideways, reaching for cover behind an equipment crate, her hand going for her radio.

Cole's eyes find mine across the chaos.

And in that moment, with bullets and accusations flying, with everything I've built crumbling around me, I realize: I would follow him anywhere.

Even into hell itself.

The 4th Law has already decided my fate. My subconscious made its choice the moment our lips touched in that container.

Now I just have to survive long enough to make it real.

---

## CHAPTER 6: THE MIDNIGHT DRYDOCK

The rain hammers down harder now, each droplet exploding like a small caliber round against my BATC-issue ballistics vest. I can taste copper and ozone on my tongue—the kind of metallic tang that means something big just went down here, recently enough that the residual magic hasn't had time to dissipate into the November air.

My boots slap through puddles deep enough to hide corpses as I move deeper into Flooded Drydock 4. The shipyard stretches out before me like a rusty cathedral, all skeletal cranes and abandoned cargo containers stacked three-high under the sickly orange glow of sodium-vapor lamps. Water reflects everything back at me doubled, tripled—a hellish funhouse where every shadow could be hiding teeth.

I'm supposed to be standing down. Vane Thorne made that crystal clear over the radio fifteen minutes ago, his British accent going sharp-edged around the edges when he said "disobeying direct orders will result in immediate suspension." But there's something here. Something that screams Cole Brennan. The temperature dropped ten degrees the moment I crossed into this section, and I can see it—the sizzling blue-black residue eating through chain-link fencing, leaving perfect tracks of iron-gall corrosion that shouldn't exist outside of theoretical thaumaturgical textbooks.

"Commander Vance to dispatch," I mutter into my collar mic, though I know damn well Thorne cut me off the moment I kept walking after his stand-down order. My words dissolve into static. Fine. Solo ops it is.

The residue leads me past stacks of rusted shipping containers, each one emblazoned with faded company logos—Maersk, Hanjin, Cosco. Global commerce's cast-off bones. My white-lilac ward flares briefly against my sternum, pushing back the damp cold that wants to sink into my marrow. But beneath it, that gray ash smell of my PTSD is getting stronger, mixing with the wet charred wool stench of my anxiety.

*Focus. Clinical. You're just doing your job.*

Then I see it: a heavy-duty padlock hanging from its hasp on a Maersk container, the steel twisted into an S-shape like someone wrung it between their fingers. And beneath where the lock used to seal the door—frost. Actual frost, spreading across the corrugated steel in crystalline patterns that glow faintly cobalt under my tactical light.

"That's new," I whisper, drawing my rune-etched MP5 from its holster. The weight settles familiar in my hands. Three-round bursts for hostiles, five if they're really fucking stupid.

I press myself against the container wall, boots silent now as I move toward the door. The frost-cobalt residue is thickest here, and there's something else—a scent underneath all the industrial decay and magical contamination. Warm hearth-coals. Home.

My wards spike suddenly, unpredictably shifting from their usual lilac-cedar signature to something entirely different. Frost-cobalt iron floods through my senses, and for a moment I'm dizzy with it, tasting copper and cinnamon while the world sharpens to an almost painful clarity.

Cole Brennan smells like coming home after a war.

"Brennan!" I call out, my voice echoing off the containers. "Federal property! Show yourself!"

Nothing but rain and distant traffic on the Pulaski Skyway.

I try the container door. Locked—that mangled padlock still somehow holding. My hand goes to the bolt cutters on my belt, but I pause. Something feels wrong about this. Too easy? Too obvious?

Then I see them—the tracks. Boot prints leading away from the door, fresh enough that the rain hasn't completely filled them. And more of that frost following them like snowflakes trailing from a blizzard.

"Commander Vance to any units—" Another attempt at comms, another burst of static. Thorne really did cut me loose.

A figure moves between containers two hundred yards out. Tall, broad-shouldered, moving with that particular lope I'd recognize anywhere even in this shit lighting.

"COLE!" My voice cracks across the yard. "This is your last chance! BATC Aegis! You're under arrest for arcano-felony, first-degree thaumaturgical assault, and conspiracy to commit—"

He's already gone around the corner, but he heard me. I can tell by the way his silhouette tensed before disappearing.

I kick the container door open without thinking, MP5 sweeping into the pitch-black interior—

—and stop dead as the barrel of a depleted-bismuth shotgun presses directly against my forehead.

The safety's already off.

* * *

The flooded drydock reeks of rust and diesel fuel. Water laps against concrete pilings somewhere below the grated walkway where I'm standing, but all I can hear is my own breathing over the hammering rain on the corrugated tin roof.

Cole Reyes materializes from the shadows like something conjured by the steam hissing from a broken pipe. His battered leather jacket catches what little sodium light bleeds through the gaps in the containers—enough for me to see the Mossberg 590A1 cradled in his arms, enough to know he's got his finger off the trigger but on the guard.

"Safety's on, Commander," he says, voice gravelly as crushed asphalt. "You're getting sloppy."

I don't flinch. My white-lilac bio-ward pushes outward, tendrils of energy seeking to blind him, disorient him—the same move that's ended three threats this month. But this time, something goes wrong. The ward crashes into an invisible wall of frost-cobalt iron that shouldn't exist, that *can't* exist unless Cole Reyes has been hiding more than just his connections to the Kearny Marshes cartel.

The impact sends a jolt up my spine. My ash-gray static, heavy with wet charred wool and the copper tang of my PTSD, simply *vanishes*. In its place comes warmth—unexpected, impossible warmth that smells of burning hearth-coals and safety and home.

"Give me one reason I don't put a burst of hollow-points through your chest, Reyes." My finger stays on the trigger. The Glock 23 feels cold against my palm, familiar weight in unfamiliar circumstances.

He doesn't lower the shotgun. Instead, he tilts his head toward the darkness behind him. "Because I saved your life at Pylon Two. And because you know that Elven wire-runner I flatlined wasn't working alone."

The rain intensifies, drumming harder against the roof. Water drips from a rusty pipe above, each drop echoing like a countdown.

"You've got five seconds to explain why you're holding federal property at gunpoint in a restricted facility."

"Four of those seconds are gonna waste while you decide whether shooting me is worth the paperwork," Cole shoots back. He shifts his weight, and I catch it—a subtle movement, not threatening but calculating. Measuring distance. Assessing options.

Then he does something I don't expect: he lowers the shotgun slowly, deliberately, and tosses it onto a wooden pallet stacked near a rusted shipping container. The metal clangs as it lands.

A Panasonic Toughbook—ruggedized model, 2007 edition with the reinforced casing—hits the grated walkway between us with a metallic thunk. Cole kicks it forward with his boot.

"Boot it up," he says. "We need to talk about Marcus Voss."

My wards flare again, but this time they're different. Still warmth. Still hearth-coals. But underneath, frost-cobalt iron threads through them like veins of ore in stone, pulsing in rhythm with my heartbeat.

I don't pick up the laptop. Not yet.

"The hell kind of bio-weave are you running, Reyes?"

* * *

The rain hammers against the corrugated steel walls of Container #472-B, each drop a percussion note in this metal tomb. I keep my Glock 23 trained on Cole's chest, but my arm's starting to shake—not from fear, but from the goddamn cold seeping through my tactical vest like liquid ice.

"Talk fast," I say, my breath fogging in the air. "Your buddy Voss has half the dockyard searching for us."

Cole leans back against the stacked crates behind him, one hand raised in mock surrender. His other hand stays tucked in his jacket—probably where he keeps whatever trick he's planning. The guy who butchered seventeen people in Sterling Manor doesn't just give up.

"The Pylons are failing," he says, voice flat as the Newark Bay outside. "Pylon #3 specifically. It's going to breach by Saturday morning. Maybe sooner if someone doesn't shut down what Voss is running."

My white-lilac wards flare, that familiar pressure building at the base of my skull. The smell hits me next—that ash-gray static mixed with wet charred wool. My PTSD playing its usual tricks.

"I'm supposed to believe you?" I pull the Toughbook from my equipment pouch, thumbs already moving across the damp keys. Windows XP boot screen flickers to life, casting sickly blue light across the container interior. "Last time we talked, you were trying to put a bullet through my partner's head."

"That was before." He shifts position, and I track the movement with my weapon. "Things changed."

"Bullshit changed." I'm typing now, pulling up satellite imagery of the Passaic River corridor. Flooding, unauthorized dredging, structural anomalies in the magical current. "You're the Butcher of Sterling Manor, Cole. You don't get to play hero just because your plans got complicated."

The container groans as wind catches it. Water drips steadily from a rust hole near the ceiling, creating rhythmic percussion. The smell inside is wrong—a mixture of stale cigarette smoke and ozone that shouldn't coexist. Magical residue.

"Voss is Visible Head Number Two," I continue, reading from the BATC dossier on my screen. "High-Spire Certified. If there's corruption at Pylon #3, Internal Affairs would have flagged it. The High-Spire arcano-compliance attorneys wouldn't allow—"

"They're not carrying briefcases, Vance."

I look up. Cole's watching me with those pale eyes, the ones that saw him through seventeen murders without blinking.

"What?"

"They're not carrying briefcases. They're carrying silenced MAC-10s with rune-etched suppressors. It's a kill-box, and they've been scrubbing the forensics every twelve hours. Standard compliance protocol, but way too frequent. Someone's paying premium rates to make sure no evidence sticks."

My wards spike again, this time different. Frost-cobalt iron threads through the white-lilac, and suddenly I can smell warm hearth-coals. My PTSD signature just... changed. That shouldn't be possible.

"You better start making sense." I lower the Glock slightly, holster it, but keep my hand ready. "Because right now you're accessory after the fact to about fifteen different crimes."

Cole pulls out a crumpled pack of Camels, shakes one loose, lights it with a Zippo that's seen better days. The flame illuminates the scars running down his jaw—old wounds, badly healed, probably self-inflicted during whatever breakdown created the Butcher.

"I need Pylon #3 offline by Friday night," he says, smoke curling around his words. "Voss is using the magical current as cover for something bigger than the Syndicate. Bigger than the BATC. If that breach happens under his operation, thousands are going to die, and the entire North Jersey infrastructure goes dark."

"Why?" The word comes out sharp. "What's your angle? Why do you suddenly give a shit about civilian casualties when you never did in Sterling Manor?"

He takes another drag, exhales slowly. Something flickers across his face—not guilt exactly, but close enough to make my trigger finger twitch.

"Let me show you something." He reaches into his jacket, and I pull my weapon back up fast. His other hand stays visible, pulling out what looks like an old PalmPilot. "Syndicate tech. Stolen from Voss's office before they caught me."

I power up my Sony MiniDisc player, pull the encrypted drive. "Talk while I verify."

The screens glow in the darkness. My Toughbook fan whirs, working overtime. Rain continues its percussion. And then our devices sync—somehow, impossibly—and the schematic renders on both screens simultaneously.

My breath catches.

"Oh god," I whisper. "Oh fucking god."

---

## CHAPTER 7: THE TWO-KEY DOOMSDAY LOCK

The container smells wrong.

Not rust and saltwater, not mildew or diesel fumes—the usual vocabulary of a Maersk box sitting cold in Newark Bay. This reeks like someone tried to burn coal inside it, left the ashes to steep for weeks. It catches in the back of my throat every time I breathe through my nose, which I've trained myself to do even in situations like this.

Cole's already inside when I slide the door open, hunched over his PalmPilot in the ambient glow from the bay lights filtering through the gaps in the metal siding. The device casts everything in that sickly green monochrome that reminds me of old emergency lighting, the kind they put in nuclear bunkers. His fingers move across the stylus in patterns I can't quite track—some kind of decryption protocol, probably Syndicate grade.

"Bringing friends?" He doesn't look up.

I step inside, letting the door clang shut behind us. The sound echoes too loud in here. "You said you had something to show me."

"The question is whether you're ready to see it." Now he looks up. Those eyes, grey as Kearny Marsh water during a fog bank, fix on me with an intensity that makes my white-lilac weave twitch involuntarily along my spine. Warmth. That fucking warmth again, radiating out from wherever the ley lines thread through my bones.

I ignore it. Professional. "Talk or walk, Cole."

He extends one hand, palm up. In it sits a frayed adapter cable, alligator clips still attached at one end, serial port connector at the other. The plastic casing has been melted and reformed around the wires—a crude but effective repair job. "Toughbook. Serial port. My PalmPilot needs to talk to your architecture files."

The MiniDisc case feels heavy in my jacket pocket. The Sony Walkman-pro model we use for field data backup—it should feel ridiculous, like something out of a tech museum, but the encryption algorithms built into our MiniDisc format are military-grade. Even now, even knowing what's coming, part of me wants to laugh at how quaint this all seems. Two people in a shipping container with obsolete technology trying to prevent the apocalypse.

I pull out the disc. It catches the light like mother-of-pearl. "What am I looking at?"

Cole takes it without asking, turns to his Toughbook already set up on a stack of crates. The ruggedized laptop boots with a mechanical whir, fan spinning up to battle the November cold seeping through the container walls. He slots the MiniDisc into the peripheral drive—there's another click-whir as the mechanism engages—and starts typing commands faster than I can follow.

"The outer seals," he says, not to me, more to himself. "BATC Aegis Protocol. Lock down the telluric pressure valves to stabilize harmonic feedback." The screen flickers, pixelated blue lines overlaying what looks like architectural schematics of Pylon #3. Newark Bay. Where we're sitting right now, essentially.

My fingers hover over the keyboard. His hands move aside without me asking. The files load, and there it is—the architectural framework for the outer seal mechanisms. Exactly what I've been working with for months. Exactly what my team has been preparing to activate when the breach reaches critical mass.

"Those are the outer seals," I say, tracing one finger along the screen edge where the blue lines converge. "My team locks them down to stabilize the harmonic feedback."

"And my crew drops the inner spikes."

The words hit different coming from him. I lean closer to see what he's doing with his PalmPilot now—he's patched it into the serial port using that melted adapter, and green monochrome data streams are merging with the Toughbook display. Red lines appear, intersecting with the blue ones in ways that make my stomach clench.

"What do you mean 'spikes'?"

Cole finally turns those grey eyes on me again. For once, there's no irony, no smirk, nothing but raw exhaustion and something worse—a kind of resigned horror. "Look at the telemetry. If the outer seals are locked when the inner spike hits..."

He doesn't need to finish. I'm already seeing it. The red lines represent some kind of internal mechanism, a series of descending spikes that would normally penetrate deep into the earth's crust to anchor the telluric pressure. But if my outer seals are engaged first, they create a dead end. A pressure differential that can only resolve one way.

"Telluric fault rupture imminent." 

The words appear in red across the bottom of the Toughbook screen, flashing with each refresh cycle. The stress-simulation runs automatically based on our merged datasets—BATC architecture meeting Syndicate operational parameters—and every model outcome scrolls past in cascading horror:

*FAULT RUPTURE: 47% PROBABILITY*
*TELLURIC FEEDBACK LOOP: CATASTROPHIC*

"The Millennium Breach isn't just about sealing the breach," Cole says quietly. His shoulder brushes mine as we both lean toward the screen, trying to absorb what we're seeing. "It's about timing. Your team activates the outer seals. My crew drops the inner spikes. They have to happen simultaneously, or..."

"Or the entire Newark Bay region experiences tectonic collapse."

I feel the warmth from my white-lilac weave spreading across my chest now, involuntary response to the adrenaline dump flooding my system. It feels like standing too close to a fire, terrifying in its comfort. Next to me, Cole radiates cold—that ten-degree drop he always carries—but somehow the combination makes sense. Hot and cold. Outer and inner. Seal and spike.

Two keys to one lock. And someone's been planning to turn both at exactly the wrong time.

"Why?" I ask, though I'm not sure who I'm asking. Him? Myself? The universe that would put us here in this moment? "Who designed it this way?"

Cole's hand comes to rest on my wrist—not quite touching, hovering close enough that I can feel the temperature difference between his skin and mine. "The same person who decided a millennium was long enough to wait for payment."

* * *

The numbers scroll across the screen, green phosphorescence bleeding into my retinas. Each line of code feels like a nail being driven into my skull.

"Wait," I say, but my fingers are already pulling up the cross-reference matrix. The thermal conductivity readings from Pylon Two. The stress analysis from Sub-Station Seven. The tectonic pressure build-up along the Neon Hollow fault line.

My stomach drops into my boots.

"Cole." My voice comes out wrong—hoarse, cracked. Like I've been screaming even though I haven't made a sound since we started this goddamn excavation.

He leans closer to the Toughbook, his frost-cobalt weave humming low in my peripheral vision. The air between us tastes like copper and ozone. His shoulder brushes mine as he brings up the projected outcomes map.

The red LED on the simulation cluster flashes failure, failure, failure.

Three hundred thousand people live above that fault line. Goblins in the splice-warrens. Orcs in the union blocks. Voss is going to flush the whole damn grid.

"The resonance cascade," I whisper, watching the numbers compound, multiply, become an equation that ends only in catastrophic collapse. "It's not just Pylon Three. It's all three pylons working in sequence. We're loading the gun while they aim it at their own fucking heads."

The smell hits me then—that phantom reek of wet charred wool and burning electronics. Sub-Station Seven. The place where my squad died because I was too slow, too stupid, too *new* to see the trap coming until it was already sprung.

"No." Cole's hand clamps down on my wrist, his skin cold enough to make my breath catch. The touch is jarring, grounding, real in a way nothing else in this container feels anymore. The charred-wool stench vanishes like someone flipped a switch.

I look up at him. His eyes are wide, pupils blown black with shock, but behind the fear there's something colder. Something that understands exactly what we're looking at.

"It's a Two-Key Doomsday Lock," he says quietly. His voice carries no inflection—just flat statement of horrifying fact. "By doing our jobs perfectly, by following the protocols they gave us, we create the conditions for the collapse. You stabilize the eastern approach. I activate the western anchor points. Together, we crack the fault line wide open."

My hands are shaking so hard the cursor jumps across the screen. I force them still, fingers white-knuckled against the keyboard.

"Then we stop. We don't touch Pylon Three. I'll pull my Aegis team. Get them out of here before—"

"You can't."

His face has gone dead-pale beneath his olive complexion. The frost-cobalt weave around him flickers, unstable.

"The activation codes were embedded in the deployment orders yesterday morning. The moment you pulled your team from active status, BATC would flag it as insubordination. Suspicion. They'd send another commander. Someone who wouldn't question. Someone who'd follow procedure."

He releases my wrist slowly, deliberately. The absence of his touch leaves my skin feeling too exposed, too vulnerable.

"And even if you could warn them... the cascade trigger is already armed. Pulling back now just means we fail to create the pressure differential. The whole western sector becomes structurally unsound. Buildings start collapsing anyway—over weeks instead of minutes. More chaos. More death. Just slower."

The words hit me like physical blows. Each one peeling back another layer of this nightmare.

"We're fucked either way." My laugh sounds wrong—hysterical, edged with something that might be tears or might be blood from where I bit my tongue. "Perfect. Absolutely goddamn perfect."

I yank the MiniDisc from its drive with enough force to crack the plastic housing. The disk clatters against the metal floor of the container, spinning lazily, reflecting the sick green glow of the screens.

"Then we burn it. Every file. Every piece of data. Make it so BATC can't use whatever bullshit they've got planned."

Cole's expression doesn't change, but his eyes dart sideways toward the door. Toward where the Maersk container sits in the middle of nowhere, surrounded by marsh and water and three hundred thousand souls living on top of a powder keg we're about to light.

"They've got remote monitoring. Kill-switch protocols. If we try to scrub the files, they'll lock us out remotely. Possibly trigger an emergency shutdown sequence that causes exactly what we're trying to prevent—a sudden collapse."

"The Syndicate?" I'm grasping at straws now, at anything that isn't this, that isn't the realization that BATC has been using me as a weapon all along. That everything I did to protect people is what will destroy them in the end.

Cole shakes his head. "Voss doesn't care about the data. He cares about the salvage—getting in after the collapse to pick through the wreckage while everyone else is still digging bodies out of the rubble. This was always BATC's play. They need someone with clearance to execute it. Someone who won't ask questions until it's too late."

The charred-wool smell returns, stronger this time. My vision starts to blur at the edges, static creeping in like frost across glass.

Sub-Station Seven again. The bodies. The screams I couldn't stop. The failure I couldn't prevent.

Not this time. Please, not this time.

"Then we run." The words feel hollow even as I say them. "We grab what we can carry and disappear into the splice-warrens. Let BATC figure out how to fix their own fuck-up."

"You know that's not how this works." Cole's voice is gentle now—not mocking, just stating fact. "You're Aegis Commander. Your team looks to you for orders. Your absence creates chaos. Panic. People make mistakes when they panic."

"People die when they follow orders," I snap back, but my heart isn't in it.

His silence is answer enough.

I slump forward against the Toughbook, forehead resting on folded arms. The screen casts sickly green shadows across my skin. Behind my closed eyes, I see the numbers again—the equation that proves we've been dancing on a razor blade this entire time, that every step forward has been another step toward annihilation.

"How long?" I ask eventually. "Before the trigger point?"

"Seventeen hours. From Pylon Three activation."

Which means tomorrow morning. During rush hour. When the streets are packed and the bridges are loaded and three hundred thousand people are going about their lives, completely unaware that we're holding the key to their tomb.

My hands find the MiniDisc again, turning it over and over between my fingers. Plastic clicking softly against plastic. A small sound in a vast and terrible quiet.

"This is insane," I whisper. "This is completely, utterly insane."

Cole says nothing. He doesn't need to. We both know there's no argument left. No other options. Just the horrifying mathematics of our situation and the

* * *

I watch him unbutton his shirt, fingers trembling—not from fear, but from the mechanical necessity of someone whose entire body has become a clockwork device for survival. The fabric parts like a wound opening, and there it is: the black corruption spreading across his chest in veins that pulse with sickening rhythm.

"The Myocardial Geas," Cole says, voice flat as he gestures to the necrotic spider-web covering his heart. "Courtesy of Dr. Aris Thorne and his 'research methodology.' Every heartbeat pushes this shit deeper into my muscles."

I lean closer despite myself, the white-lilac weave humming against my skin where our shoulders nearly touch. The geometric patterns shift and flow, responding to something primal—the need to understand, to diagnose, to heal. But I can't heal this. Nobody can.

The black veins branch outward from his sternum like a map of hell, each tributary ending in what looks like small cauterized wounds. Ozone seeps from them—sharp, sterile, wrong. This isn't natural magic. This is something else entirely.

"If I stop feeding it mana, if I even think about aborting the mission, the Geas ruptures." His hand moves to trace one of the darker lines, and I see how it throbs under his touch. "There's a brass-and-glass iron lung keeping my brother Danny alive. Eighteen years old. Coma since the accident at the Passaic River plant. If I drop the spike, the lung shuts off, and he drowns in his own blood."

My stomach lurches. The Nextel pager on my belt chirps insistently—a routine status update from Sub-Station 38. Thirty-eight orphans. Twenty-three metahuman. All warded by me personally.

"Show me," I say, already pulling up my own command interface with shaking fingers.

The files load. And there it is, buried in the subroutine I'd accepted without question three weeks ago: **HARMONIC DAMPENING WARD - REVERSE-GEAS PROTOCOL**. BATC standard procedure. For our protection, they said. To prevent feedback loops during high-stress operations.

I was such a fool.

"They wired the kids to my Aegis mandate," I whisper, reading the cascading failure protocols. "If I don't seal the Pylon, if I fail this mission, the feedback loop cooks their nervous systems. Burns them out from the inside like faulty Christmas lights."

Cole buttons his shirt slowly, methodically. Each button click sounds final. "And if I don't drop the spike, my brother drowns in his own blood. They made sure we'd both turn the keys, didn't they? Gave us no choice but to play along with their little apocalypse."

The container suddenly feels smaller, darker. The coal-smoke scent intensifies—old magic, old power, old lies wrapped around new horrors. My white-lilac weave pulses warmer against my skin, almost alive, almost sentient. It wants to comfort. Wants to wrap around Cole's chest and heal what cannot be healed.

Wants things that terrify me.

My pulse hammers against my ribs. I check it manually—sixty-two beats per minute. Too fast for tactical calm. The Geas on the orphans doesn't need mana to maintain. Just needs me to fail. Just needs me to die, even. The protocol triggers automatically.

"Thirty-eight children," I say, forcing my voice steady even as my throat constricts. "How old is your brother?"

"Eighteen." He meets my eyes, and there's something ancient in his gaze—not the boy who looks fifteen, but something that survived too much too young. "Same age as half those kids probably."

A metallic *CLANG* echoes outside the container. Sharp. Authoritative. Something heavy hitting metal.

The Nextel pager erupts into a continuous high-pitched warning tone.

Perimeter breach.

We lock eyes over the glowing screens between us, and I see the same calculation running behind his: do we run, do we fight, do we finish what they've programmed us to do?

Outside, footsteps. Multiple sets. Getting closer.

---

## CHAPTER 8: THE GEAS & THE SLIVER OF JUSTICE

I press my palms flat against Cole's chest, feeling the frantic drumbeat of his heart through the tactical vest. My white-lilac weave spirals outward from my sternum—defensive protocols screaming warnings that I silence with sheer willpower.

The Geas glows beneath his skin like infected veins, frost-cobalt lightning branching across his ribs. Ancient magic. Corporate blood-law from when the High Spires still held dominion over Jersey's eastern coast. My fingers hover an inch above the first pulse-point, already feeling the heat radiating off it.

"Tell me again," I say, voice tight. "Exactly how it works."

Cole's jaw clenches. His shotgun rests against his shoulder, barrels pointed at the container's far wall. Outside, boots splash through puddles—the BATC cleanup team making their sweep. We have maybe five minutes before they check this unit.

"The Myocardial Geas is keyed to cardiac arrest," he says, clinical despite the tremor in his hands. "If my heart stops, if I go into arrest for more than forty seconds, the fail-deadly triggers. The fault line drops. Three hundred thousand people die in the tidal surge."

My fingers find the first necrotic pulse-point. The moment my skin makes contact, magic *screams* through me. Black burn spreads across my fingertips, cedar smoke rising from flesh that shouldn't be burning but does anyway. I grit my teeth hard enough to taste copper.

"It's tied to a blood-registry." I pull back, examining the spreading necrosis on my right hand. Already bubbling, already dying. "Elven notary seal. Corporate law from the First Accord." I look up at Cole, forcing eye contact even as my left hand trembles. "I can't break this without triggering it. It's designed to make sure nobody can save you."

The container reeks of ozone and rust. Water drips somewhere overhead. Each sound feels like a countdown.

"So we're trapped." I'm running clinical triage protocols in my head—every loophole, every magical precedent, every fucking technicality the Academy hammered into me over eight years. Nothing. The blood-law is ironclad. Corporate contracts written by beings who understood suffering as an art form.

Cole's eyes are hollow when he looks at me. "There's one way out."

"You'll do it yourself?" My voice cracks. "You have a bypass?"

"No." He racks his shotgun—an unnecessary gesture, the click echoing off metal walls. "We play our parts perfectly. Then we make them pay."

I slam my good hand against the container wall, sending a cascade of water bottles clattering. "So what? We just do it? We drop the fault line and kill three hundred thousand people to save thirty-nine?"

The question hangs between us like a corpse.

Outside, boots stop. Someone's talking into a radio, voice muffled by distance. The cleanup team is getting close.

"There has to be another way," I whisper, but I know. I've known since the moment I felt that High-Spire signature threading through Cole's heart. This was never meant to be survivable. It's a trap door built for one purpose: ensure compliance through impossible choices.

My white-lilac weave flares desperately, casting shadows across both our faces. I push harder, deeper, burning myself out searching for any crack in the Geas's architecture. The necrotic feedback intensifies. My left hand is already a ruin, black tissue spreading up my wrist.

Still nothing. No loopholes. No abort mechanisms. Just the cold mathematics of sacrifice.

Cole watches me burn myself trying to find an escape that doesn't exist. His expression never changes.

"We don't have time for this, Little Halo."

* * *

The Toughbook screen flickers one last time before dying completely, casting us into near-darkness. Only the faint bioluminescence of our respective weaves cuts through the gloom—my white-lilac defense still humming at maximum capacity, Cole's frost-cobalt sparks dancing like malevolent fireflies across his shoulders.

I keep the Mossberg trained on him. My hands don't shake. They haven't shaken since I pulled this trigger on Marcus Voss.

"You've killed dozens of people, Cole." My voice comes out flat, mechanical. Like I'm reading from a script I didn't write. "You think killing Voss is going to balance the scales? It's not justice."

He stands there in the darkness, a silhouette against the metal walls of the shipping container. Rain hammers down on the corrugated steel above us, each drop sounding like gunfire.

"I know it's not." 

His words are soft. Deceptively soft. The kind of soft that precedes the worst things people can say to each other.

"The sliver of justice is never enough, Vance." He takes a step forward, and I feel my finger tighten fractionally on the trigger. His weave flares brighter, those fucking cobalt sparks making my teeth ache. "It doesn't scrape the black iron out of an eighteen-year-old kid's lungs. It doesn't bring back the dead."

Another step. Closer now. Close enough that I can smell the ozone radiating off his skin, mixed with motor oil and blood.

"But it will do for the moment. Because a sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone."

The shotgun shells clack as I pump the action—not threatening, just habit. Reassurance. A sound I understand in a world that suddenly makes less sense than five minutes ago.

"What happened to your brother isn't justice," I say, but even as the words leave my mouth, they taste wrong. Hollow. Because what am I defending here? What system am I championing when Marcus Voss was still breathing thirty seconds ago?

Cole's laugh is bitter, sharp. Like glass breaking in winter.

"Justice?" He shakes his head slowly, deliberately. "I gave up on justice when I watched my brother choke on his own blood in some shithole clinic in Kearny while Voss drank champagne at the Mariners Club. You want to talk about systems, Commander? Your system let that happen. My brother died because your 'justice' couldn't reach past the velvet rope."

He moves again—fast this time—and before I can react he's right there, close enough that I could see the individual frost crystals forming along his jawline if there were any light worth shit.

"You know what keeps me going through all this?" His voice drops lower, intimate in its horror. "What gets me through the nights after I've done... things?"

I don't answer. Can't.

"It's not revenge, Vance. Not anymore." Another step. We're almost touching now, separated only by inches of charged air. "Revenge would be killing everyone who ever looked at Voss sideways. Revenge would be burning this whole fucking city down until the ashes match what's left of my lungs."

The container lurches. A grinding metallic groan echoes through the space around us.

"That's not it though." Cole's eyes lock onto mine and I swear I can see ice forming in them. "It's the Sliver. The Threefold Cord my father taught me before the black iron took him."

Outside, something thunders against the container wall. Hard. Deliberate.

"Aegis Commander Vance!" A voice cuts through the rain, amplified and sharp. "This is Voss Security. Step out of the container and surrender the mechanic!"

Cole doesn't even flinch. Just keeps staring at me like we're the only two people in the world.

"Penance," he says quietly, as if the megaphone never existed. "Every kill weighs on me, Mara. Every soul I drag into the deep. That's penance."

His hand comes up slowly—so slowly—and places itself flat against the barrel of my shotgun. I could fire right now. Should fire. But I don't because some part of me needs to hear this.

"And revenge." His fingers curl around the metal, steady as a rock. "That's easy. You know about that one already."

The megaphone blares again: *"You have sixty seconds before we breach! Surrender the suspect!"*

"I've got forty seconds to tell you the last part," Cole says calmly, conversationally, like we're discussing the weather over coffee. "And here's the ugly truth you won't want to hear: Justice isn't balance, Vance. It's not scales or ledgers or any of that bullshit they teach you at the Academy."

He pulls the shotgun down gently but firmly until the muzzle points at the floor between us.

"The sliver of justice is what remains when you've carved away everything else. After the rage burns out and the guilt settles cold in your gut, there's a tiny piece left over. A shard of something that means *something*."

Another tremor shakes the entire container. The sound of servos whining, hydraulic arms engaging.

*"Thirty seconds!"*

"I killed Marcus Voss today," Cole says, and for the first time since I met him, his voice cracks slightly. Just barely. "I took a life. Destroyed something irreplaceable. And I'll answer for it—God help me, I'll answer for it."

His other hand comes up to cover mine on the Mossberg grip.

"But tonight, right now, in this moment?" He squeezes my hand hard enough to hurt. "Tonight I'm looking at an Aegis Commander who just committed the same sin I live with every day. Who pulled the trigger on justice instead of waiting for the law. Who felt that same sliver of something true cut through all the training and protocol."

The megaphone: *"TEN SECONDS! BREACH IN TEN!"*

"Justice isn't fair," Cole whispers urgently now as the countdown continues outside. "It's not clean or righteous or noble. It's a sliver, Mara. Just a fucking sliver. But it's real."

He releases my hands, steps back into the shadows.

"And sometimes a sliver is all we get."

* * *

The rusted bullet hole offers me only fragments—a sliver of the world beyond this steel tomb. Through it, I see the dance of tactical flashlights cutting through sheets of November rain like surgical blades. A dozen silhouettes move with practiced efficiency, PMC contractors in black tactical gear spreading out across the Maersk yard in perfect formation.

My white-lilac weave constricts around my chest, each breath now measured, controlled. The frost-cobalt sparks dancing at the edges of my awareness—Cole's proximity effect—should trigger panic. Should send me spiraling back to those nights after Newark Bay. But they don't. Instead, they burn away the static, sharpen everything into crystal focus.

"Commander Vance." The voice cuts through the rain-slicked darkness, amplified, artificial perfection wrapping around words meant to paralyze. One of the High-Spire attorneys steps forward, charcoal suit immaculate beneath the transparent raincoat, silver warrant-stylus held at his side. The device hums—high-pitched, insectoid—charging with kinetic magic that makes my teeth ache.

You are in violation of a Class-A Corporate Non-Disclosure. Surrender your sidearm and the Panasonic Toughbook.

I don't answer him. My eyes lock on Cole, watching his face in the strobing light. The grenade appears in his hand as if summoned from air itself—not the careful movement of someone reaching for equipment, but something older. Practiced. He pulls the pin with his thumb, holds it loose in his palm like it weighs nothing.

"They aren't here to arrest us," I tell him, keeping my voice level even as my MP5's fire-selector clicks from semi to full-auto. Metal on polymer. A sound I've heard a thousand times before combat, ten thousand more during it. "They're here to scrub the site."

The second attorney moves closer, her stylus drawing lazy circles through the rain-soaked air. Each pass sends ripples of force across the container walls—I feel them reverberate through my bones, taste copper where my gums bleed slightly from the pressure. This isn't about containment anymore. This is extermination dressed up in corporate legality.

Then they move.

Both attorneys drag their styluses upward in perfect synchronization, and the world *explodes* inward. Kinetic force—a wall of compressed air that shouldn't exist outside of focused demolition charges—slams into our shelter. The corrugated steel doors don't just open. They *vaporize*, torn clean off their hinges by the concussive wave, hurling themselves into the darkness like wounded birds.

Rain cascades into our space, immediate and cold.

Cole's arm comes around me, not gentle—pushing me back deeper into the container as tactical rounds stitch across the opening where the doors used to be. The sound is obscene: a sustained crack-crack-crack that vibrates in my sternum. PMC assault rifles, probably FN SCAR-Hs firing 7.62mm rounds designed to punch through light armor.

I return fire without thinking, my MP5 bucking against my shoulder, sending a stream of 9mm parabellum rounds toward the flashpoints. One contractor drops. Then another. But there are too many angles, too much open ground between us and any kind of cover.

"Grenade out!" Cole shouts it, but he's already throwing—not at the attackers, but at the far end of the container where we'd been hiding. It rolls across wet metal, and I understand his intention a half-second before impact.

The explosion rips through our makeshift shelter, detonating in controlled chaos. Shrapnel scatters, tearing through the container walls in multiple directions. Smoke billows outward, obscuring vision for the PMCs outside while simultaneously providing concealment.

I'm moving before the smoke clears, yanking the Toughbook from its cradle and stuffing it inside my armored vest against my spine. My free hand keeps the MP5 trained on the opening, watching shapes shift in the smoke-veil beyond. Someone screams—a wet, gurgling sound cut short by more gunfire.

"Vance! Move!" Cole's already at the tear in the container wall, the one made by the kinetic blast. He fires back into the darkness, methodical bursts meant to suppress rather than kill. "We're pinned. We need—"

The second kinetic blast hits us broadside.

Not aimed directly at us, but close enough that I feel my eardrums pop, taste blood from a bitten tongue. The container itself groans—the entire structure shifting on its supports as steel buckles and twists under focused force. More tactical fire pours into our position.

Cole grabs me by the collar, hauls me through the torn metal toward what might be an exit or might just be another killing zone. I can't tell anymore. Can't think past the adrenaline firing every synapse in my brain.

Behind us, the High-Spire attorneys are advancing, their styluses drawing patterns of destruction through rain-slicked air. Corporate justice rendered in violence so precise it might as well be magic. Which, technically, it is.

The frost-cobalt sparks around Cole intensify—bright enough now to cast shadows across the ruined container interior. His doctrine, whatever it is, whatever he confessed while I was supposed to be listening instead of cataloging threats—I'll have time to understand it later.

Or not.

Because we're out in the open now, and the Maersk yard stretches before us like a killing ground lit by tactical flashlights that turn everything monochrome and vicious. The Pulaski Skyway looms in the distance, its elevated concrete ribbons disappearing into fog that rolls off the Passaic River like something breathing.

I count four active shooters. Maybe more. The Elven attorneys are twenty meters behind us, moving with confidence that suggests they know exactly how this ends.

"Left flank," I call out, seeing movement near the shipping office. "Cover three o'clock."

Cole pivots without hesitation, his own weapon coming up as he fires toward the new contact. A figure drops—not one of ours—and for a moment there's confusion among the attackers.

We run toward it.

Not strategy. Instinct. The desperate mathematics of survival when you've already calculated your odds and found them unacceptable.

The ground beneath our feet turns treacherous, mud from recent rains mixing with oil slicks and God knows what else bleeding from ruptured containers. My boots slip twice in ten steps, each time catching myself just short of falling hard enough to break something vital.

Behind us: the high-pitched whine of charging kinetic magic, growing louder.

Ahead: darkness and rain and the distant promise of escape routes we haven't planned yet because planning requires time we don't have.

My white-lilac weave burns against my ribs, defensive postures cycling through their sequences as my training tries to compensate for impossible situations. Frost-cobalt sparks cast dancing shadows across Cole's face—sharp angles and harder eyes.

He glances at me while running, says something I can't hear over gunfire and rain.

I shake my head. Can't understand. Keep moving.

The third kinetic blast

## CHAPTER 9: BACK-TO-BACK IN THE RAIN

The frag rounds out of my MP5 before I even register the threat—a double-tap to center mass that punches through tactical vests like paper. Blood fans across the rain-slicked asphalt in arterial sprays, human mercs crumpling without so much as a death cry. The downpour swallows their bodies whole.

"Contact right!" Cole's voice cuts through the storm.

I pivot left, muscle memory older than thought. My boot catches on something—warm, yielding. A throat. The Ogre-kin breacher goes down hard, his riot shield clattering against rusted shipping containers stacked like tombstones. Steam rises where blood meets rain, copper stench mixing with cordite and burning nylon from shredded raincoats.

"Stack up! Watch the arcane backblast!" Someone yells behind the containers. Professional. Organized.

"We're pinned!" Another voice, younger. Scared.

My MP5 stutters. Dry. "Shit."

Cole materializes beside me, somehow there despite the chaos, tossing a fresh magazine from his combat vest. Our hands meet mid-air—the exchange so practiced it feels like breathing. I slam home the mag, chamber a round.

BOOM.

A grenade detonates somewhere to our left. The drydock shudders. Metal screams. Rain drums harder against the corrugated iron roof overhead.

"Impact! Fifty meters—east quadrant!" The tactical net crackles in my ear, but it's not ours. Enemy comms. They think they've got us boxed.

Cole grabs my arm, frost already crystallizing along his fingertips. His eyes catch mine—those weird amber irises reflecting the distant Newark Bay lights like lighthouse beacons. "Move for the gantry! I'll cover the flank!"

No time to question. We explode forward as one unit, boots slapping wet asphalt that offers zero traction. My feet slide out—oil slick beneath the rain—and I catch myself against a rusted winch mechanism, vault over it in a desperate scramble.

Three-round burst. Center mass on the breacher whose kneecap Cole just turned into ground beef. The Ogre-kin staggers, shield falling, neck exposed. My shots walk up his throat. Blood geysers. He drops.

"Clip's dry, slot the backup!" I'm already moving, ejecting the spent mag even as new rounds feed into the weapon.

More shapes emerge from behind the containers—human mercs, at least four of them, spreading into firing positions. Black tactical gear, helmets with night vision optics. Professional hitters.

"They're trying to funnel us toward the waterline!" Cole's reading the same battlefield calculus I am. Kill box. Classic geometry. They want us trapped between their positions and the Passaic River.

The gantry crane looms ahead—a skeleton of steel and chain hoists suspended above Drydock 4. If we can reach its base, we have high ground. Cover. A chance.

Lightning splits the sky. Thunder follows immediately. The rain intensifies to biblical levels.

I see him then—the High-Spire Elven attorney standing atop the control cabin for the crane. His stylus glows with arcane fire, tracing runes in the air with impossible precision despite the wind and rain. Behind him, two more elves in expensive suits watch like spectators at some brutal theater.

"No!" I scream, but it's too late.

The elf points his stylus directly at our position. The crane's main cables sing—a sound like harp strings being cut. Steel snaps. Hooks release.

Three tons of shipping container begins its descent.

I look up just in time to see my death plummeting toward me, and there's no time to move, no cover close enough, nothing except—

Cole slams into me from the side, both of us tumbling across wet asphalt, rain hammering our faces, the world spinning until we crash behind a stack of wooden pallets that somehow, impossibly, are still upright.

The container hits where we stood moments before. Metal crumples with a sound like God closing a door. Shockwave ripples through the drydock. Pallet wood splinters explode outward.

My ears ring. Everything tastes like blood and copper.

"Mara!" Cole's shaking my shoulder, pulling me back from shock. "We need to move! They'll be on top of us!"

Behind him, through gaps in the splintered pallets, I can make out the elves on the control cabin. They're not moving forward. Not coming down to finish the job themselves. This was always the plan—to drop the weight, then let their hired guns clean up.

Cowards. All of them.

But I can't afford contempt right now. Only survival.

"How many rounds left?" I check my MP5. Ten in the magazine. Plus the spare on my vest. Twenty shots against how many threats?

Cole checks his own weapon—a modified revolver that fires depleted-bismuth slugs designed specifically for metahuman kills. Five shots. He reloads with practiced efficiency.

"Sixteen total." His answer says everything. We're fighting a losing battle here.

Lightning flashes again. In its brief illumination, I count at least six mercs advancing between shipping containers, weapons raised. They think they've won. That we're pinned. Cornered.

They don't know about the third exit. The one mapped during my recon sweep three days ago.

"Follow me," I tell Cole, already moving low along the dock's edge. "There's maintenance access two hundred meters south. Underwater intake for the ballast systems."

"If it's flooded—"

"It's our only shot."

The mercs haven't noticed our movement yet. Still focused on where the container hit. Professional mistake—they're looking at what they expect rather than what is.

We reach the access hatch. Grated steel, rusted but intact. I yank it open and dive inside, Cole right behind me. The ladder descends into darkness punctuated by dim red emergency lighting.

Behind us, someone finally notices. "Contact! South perimeter!"

Gunfire erupts, rounds pinging off the drydock's concrete walls. One hits the ladder rung beside my hand, sparks flying.

I drop faster, feet finding rungs blindly, rain still hammering down from above mixing with the metallic taste of fear in my mouth.

We need to reach the water. Need to disappear before they realize what we're doing.

Need to survive this night.

But as my boots touch submerged concrete below, I know the real hunt is just beginning.

* * *

The container fell like a guillotine.

I threw my hands up without thinking, every fiber of my training screaming through my nerves as I projected a massive white-lilac bio-ward between us and that ton-of-death dropping from the crane's severed cables. The ward materialized—iridescent petals of force blooming in the air—but it was like catching a collapsing building with your bare hands.

The kinetic weight slammed into my weave and my knees buckled immediately, my boots scraping across wet concrete as I fought for purchase. My shoulder joints screamed. My spine compressed. The ward flickered, straining at its seams, and I could feel reality beginning to tear around the edges where my magic couldn't contain the physics of a forty-foot steel box falling on top of us.

"I can't hold it!" The scream tore from my throat raw and desperate.

Something slammed into my back—not an attack, but a body. Solid. Warm. Cole's chest pressed against my shoulder blades as he braced himself behind me, driving his feet into the ground. His frost-cobalt blood-iron weave erupted outward, tendrils of crystalline blue-white energy seeking anchor points.

"Push it through me!" he shouted over the groan of tearing metal above.

I didn't have time to question. Survival instinct took over. I ripped open the channels between our signatures—the merge point we'd established during the Passaic River ambush, when his dying had become my strength and vice versa. His blood-iron magic poured *through* my white-lilac wards like water finding a new riverbed.

The synthesis exploded outward.

Warm hearth-coals. That's what it smelled like—suddenly, impossibly—that rich, comforting scent of a fire in winter overpowering the acrid cordite still hanging in the air from earlier gunfire. The two magics fused so perfectly they might have been designed together: my organic bio-warding and his metallic blood-weaving creating something neither of us could have manifested alone.

White-lilac petals now edged with frost-cobalt crystals spiraled outward in a sphere that swallowed the falling container entirely. There was no deflection, no redirection—I simply refused to let physics apply to us. The container's momentum transferred through our combined weave, and reality itself seemed to buckle under the strain before snapping back.

Metal shrieked. The container tore apart like tissue paper caught in a hurricane, jagged sections of steel scattering across the flooded drydock in a storm of harmless shrapnel. Each piece tumbled into the black water with hollow splashes.

The light from our fusion burned so bright it seared my retinas even through half-closed eyes. For one perfect moment, Cole and I stood locked together—backs pressed tight, breathing synchronized, our merged aura pulsing outward in waves of warmth against the November cold and rain.
